summary: INT014 is a 73-year-old Eaton Fire survivor whose recovery is dominated by three compounding crises: total home loss, a JPL layoff after 17 years, and the fire-triggered medical deterioration of his wife, who has late-stage Alzheimer's. When the fires hit he was already his wife's sole caregiver approaching his limits; evacuation trauma so severely destabilized her that she required successive hospitalizations, a convalescent stay, and ultimately permanent memory care placement now over an hour away in Murrieta. This transformation of his caregiving role brought both relief and guilt — she is professionally cared for, but he cannot visit as often as he would like. In the acute phase he ran on adrenaline; once things stabilized, profound exhaustion set in — he now sleeps ten-plus hours a day and starts afternoons around noon. Housing displacement moved from a FEMA hotel to a donated RV parked in Northridge to a rental that works well for him and his pets. Insurance was smooth — he explicitly notes this as fortunate compared to others. He contracted with a rebuild team he trusts, made the decision to rebuild only on the condition it would be fun, and anticipates stressful moments ahead. His JPL layoff — the first time in his career he did not choose to leave a job — is an ongoing wound, though retirement income provides financial stability. He continues working on science papers and conference abstracts from a personal laptop as an intellectual lifeline. Technology use for recovery has been modest: a WhatsApp group with neighbors on a nearby street, and the JPL Disaster Recovery Support Group via Zoom (initially in-person access was revoked with a retiree badge, which he experienced as institutional insult, before being readmitted virtually). He has never used AI and is genuinely skeptical of it for emotional support — he wants human in-person therapy — but sees real potential for practical AI assistance in contractor comparison, rebuild logistics, and eventually locating closer memory care for his wife. When the MVP concept was described, he endorsed it for practical recovery tasks, named a decision support tool as his specific feature wish, and drew a firm line at AI for emotional processing. He closes with a generational observation: younger survivors, more comfortable with voice assistants, would likely find the tool more naturally useful.
